messages.author: 1356bff10164b43d
messages.subject: update on uniformly sampling a convex polytope
parts:
I posted a question last week about uniformly sampling a convex polytope with Stan:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/YCCOuUO4jgc

I am really thankful for the responses from the Stan community. Below is the code I currently use to sample points from a 20-dimensional simplex:

library(rstan)
library(MASS)
A <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = 20)
b <- 1
dim(b) <- 1
Ag <- ginv(A)
code <-'data {
  int<lower=1> m;
  int<lower=1> n;
  vector[m] b;
  matrix[m,n] A;
  matrix[n,m] Ag;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[n,n] ImAgA;
  vector[n] Agb;
  Agb <- Ag * b;
  ImAgA <- -Ag*A;
  for(i in 1:n) ImAgA[i,i] <- ImAgA[i,i] + 1.0;
}
parameters {
  vector[n] w;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[n] x;
  x <- Agb + ImAgA * w;
}
model {
}'
d <- list(m = 1, n = 20, b = b, A = A, Ag = Ag)
fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000)
x <- extract(fit)$x

Except for some uninvited informational messages (running R from cmd does partially solve the problem as Ben kindly suggests), the sampling looks alright. So I went on to evaluate the sampling quality using coda package which implements Gelman-Rubin diagnostic. I created five mcmc objects with methods in the coda package, each from a single chain with 1000 points. Then I combined them into a mcmc list and passed it to Gelman - Rubin test. Here is the specific code:

library(coda)
m1 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m2 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m3 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m4 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m5 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
mclist.stan <- mcmc.list(m1, m2, m3, m4, m5)
gelman.diag(mclist.stan, multivariate = FALSE)

According to my understanding, an upper bound of 1 for Gelman-Rubin statistic indicates good mixing while a result substantially larger than 1 implies poor convergence. Below is what I got for each of the 20 dimensions (first column shows point estimates and second column shows the upper limit of 95% C.I.):

      Point est. Upper C.I.
 [1,]       1.81       3.19
 [2,]       1.39       1.97
 [3,]       2.19       4.28
 [4,]       1.25       1.59
 [5,]       1.10       1.25
 [6,]       1.22       1.58
 [7,]       1.65       2.70
 [8,]       2.42       5.13
 [9,]       1.08       1.22
[10,]       1.44       2.02
[11,]       1.18       1.49
[12,]       2.13       3.71
[13,]       2.00       3.62
[14,]       1.13       1.30
[15,]       1.84       3.08
[16,]       1.22       1.66
[17,]       2.43       4.28
[18,]       2.37       4.83
[19,]       1.22       1.59
[20,]       2.06       3.32

I accidentally came across another package - limSolve - with a function called "xsample" which does exactly uniform sampling under linear constraints. For default setting, "xsample" adopts mirror algorithm which "uses the inequality constraints as reflecting planes along which jumps are reflected" and thus has an exponential complexity with respect to input dimensions. Below is how I approached the same 20-dimensional simplex sampling problem with "xsample" in limSolve package and how I examined its performance:

library(limSolve)
dimen <- 20
E <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = dimen)
F <- c(1)
G <- diag(1, nrow = dimen, ncol = dimen)
H <- matrix(0, nrow = dimen, ncol = 1)
s1 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s2 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s3 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s4 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s5 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
mclist.xsam <- mcmc.list(s1, s2, s3, s4, s5)
gelman.diag(mclist.xsam, multivariate = FALSE)

And here is the Gelman-Rubin test score for sampling with limSolve:

      Point est. Upper C.I.
 [1,]       1.00       1.00
 [2,]       1.00       1.01
 [3,]       1.01       1.01
 [4,]       1.02       1.03
 [5,]       1.00       1.01
 [6,]       1.00       1.01
 [7,]       1.01       1.02
 [8,]       1.00       1.01
 [9,]       1.00       1.00
[10,]       1.00       1.01
[11,]       1.00       1.01
[12,]       1.00       1.01
[13,]       1.00       1.00
[14,]       1.00       1.01
[15,]       1.00       1.01
[16,]       1.00       1.01
[17,]       1.00       1.00
[18,]       1.00       1.00
[19,]       1.00       1.00
[20,]       1.00       1.00

Maybe it's my fault, but it does appear that "xsample" outperforms Stan by this measure. However, I really want to use Stan to solve my uniform sampling problem (not just from simplex but more generally from convex polytope), because Stan seems more systematic and professional at sampling various distributions. I wonder if there should be some smarter ways of tackling this problem with Stan.

I saw in the forum FAQ that adding a new distribution to Stan with C++ is easy, so can uniform sampling be cracked this way? I also learned that Stan's sampling scheme over a finite interval consists of mapping the interval to some unconstrained space and then using logistic sampler before finally converting the sampled result back to the designated interval. Will this process get in the way of uniformity? Or maybe we can just add some tailored functionality to Stan for a more satisfactory solution?

The above paragraph is just my random thoughts which may or may not be relevant. Again, every suggestion on the central problem of better sampling the positive solution space of Ax=b with Stan is greatly appreciated.

On Monday, July 28, 2014 8:49:06 PM UTC-4, Yuanchu Dang wrote:

I posted a question last week about uniformly sampling a convex polytope with Stan:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/YCCOuUO4jgc

Mike had some nice explanations on the stan-dev list:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Sc5PwZaE8fQ/Gsue505VfMcJ

Certainly, if you were only interested in sampling from a simplex, there are easier and more efficient ways to do that in Stan. But if, as I suspected, you are ultimately interested in problems where there is no explicit or implicit (given A and b) constraint on the sum of x, then I don't know how else to approach the convex polytope problem.

I am really thankful for the responses from the Stan community. Below is the code I currently use to sample points from a 20-dimensional simplex:

library(rstan)
library(MASS)
A <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = 20)
b <- 1
dim(b) <- 1
Ag <- ginv(A)
code <-'data {
  int<lower=1> m;
  int<lower=1> n;
  vector[m] b;
  matrix[m,n] A;
  matrix[n,m] Ag;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[n,n] ImAgA;
  vector[n] Agb;
  Agb <- Ag * b;
  ImAgA <- -Ag*A;
  for(i in 1:n) ImAgA[i,i] <- ImAgA[i,i] + 1.0;
}
parameters {
  vector[n] w;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[n] x;
  x <- Agb + ImAgA * w;
}
model {
}'
d <- list(m = 1, n = 20, b = b, A = A, Ag = Ag)
fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000)
x <- extract(fit)$x

Except for some uninvited informational messages (running R from cmd does partially solve the problem as Ben kindly suggests),

If (and only if) you know for sure (as in this case) that the informational messages are not very informative. Then you could also get around them by doing

...
parameters {
  vector[n] w;
}
model {
  vector[n] x;
x <- Agb + ImAgA * w;

for(i in 1:n) if(x[i] < 0) increment_log_prob(negative_infinity());
}
generated quantities {
  vector[n] x;

x <- Agb + ImAgA * w;
}

the sampling looks alright.

Not in this case. If you just print the fit object, you can see a calculation of the Gelman-Rubin statistic (without degrees of freedom corrections that coda does but with splitting the chains which coda does not do). You can ignore those for w, but the ones for x do not look good in this case (or even with iter=10000).

Maybe it's my fault, but it does appear that "xsample" outperforms Stan by this measure. However, I really want to use Stan to solve my uniform sampling problem (not just from simplex but more generally from convex polytope), because Stan seems more systematic and professional at sampling various distributions. I wonder if there should be some smarter ways of tackling this problem with Stan.

For a simplex problem, you can just do

parameters {
  simplex[n] x;
}
model {

}

but I doubt that is of much help to you for general A and b.

I saw in the forum FAQ that adding a new distribution to Stan with C++ is easy, so can uniform sampling be cracked this way? I also learned that Stan's sampling scheme over a finite interval consists of mapping the interval to some unconstrained space and then using logistic sampler
logistic transformation, although in this case there are no transformations of w.

before finally converting the sampled result back to the designated interval. Will this process get in the way of uniformity? Or maybe we can just add some tailored functionality to Stan for a more satisfactory solution?

It is still uniform in the constrained space (x), although not uniform in the unconstrained space (w). I don't know what to do from here, you can concentrate the distribution of w with some prior to get more efficient sampling, but then the distribution of x would not be uniform among positive solutions to Ax = b. Maybe someone else has an idea.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] update on uniformly sampling a convex polytope
parts:
I’m not sure I understand why Stan would be the right choice for this — in the case of a single
column-A matrix and positive x you can construct the simplex analytically and sample from
a Dirichlet over that simplex directly, using the usual normalized gamma variates (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution#Random_number_generation) or
(n - 1) draws from a Beta distribution (http://arxiv.org/abs/1010.3436).  MCMC shouldn’t
be necessary for this relatively simple problem.

In the case of multiple constraints you have to figure out the constrained space (the intersection
of multiple simplices) which Stan wouldn’t be able to do anyways, but could be worked out
analytically with enough effort.

messages.subject: Re: update on uniformly sampling a convex polytope
parts:
Thanks again, Mr. Goodrich, for your response! You are absolutely right that I want to sample from the positive solutions of Ax=b in general, not just a n-dimensional simplex. 

The code does work in getting rid of the messages, and I am reading your thread and Mr. Betancourt's reply on that further.

I can see now that the GR statistic is poor when I print "fit". In fact, I got roughly the same diagnostic with coda (although I did have to pass multiple chains to it manually since, like you said, coda cannot identify different chains by itself)

Also, your comment about the sampling of w is very helpful. My current understanding is that we need to sample w uniformly from an unconstrained space in order to do uniform sampling of x, but Stan is not able to sample w uniformly in the first place. However, you mentioned that if uniformity is not required then adding some priors to w will make the sampling more efficient. I guess I may actually take that option if it really works, since my application of this whole sampling project is to generate a bunch of diverse portfolios that fulfill some designated constraints. It might be the case that although ideal uniformity cannot be achieved, the diversity obtained with the approach of adding priors to concentrate w is good enough for my purpose. Could you show me how to do that?

Much thanks!

Yuanchu

...

Not in this case. If you just print the fit object, you can see a calculation of the Gelman-Rubin statistic (without degrees of freedom corrections that coda does but with splitting the chains which coda does not do). You can ignore those for w, but the ones for x do not look good in this case (or even with iter=10000).
 
Maybe it's my fault, but it does appear that "xsample" outperforms Stan by this measure. However, I really want to use Stan to solve my uniform sampling problem (not just from simplex but more generally from convex polytope), because Stan seems more systematic and professional at sampling various distributions. I wonder if there should be some smarter ways of tackling this problem with Stan.

For a simplex problem, you can just do

parameters {
  simplex[n] x;
}
model {

}

but I doubt that is of much help to you for general A and b.
 
I saw in the forum FAQ that adding a new distribution to Stan with C++ is easy, so can uniform sampling be cracked this way? I also learned that Stan's sampling scheme over a finite interval consists of mapping the interval to some unconstrained space and then using logistic sampler

logistic transformation, although in this case there are no transformations of w.
 
before finally converting the sampled result back to the designated interval. Will this process get in the way of uniformity? Or maybe we can just add some tailored functionality to Stan for a more satisfactory solution?

It is still uniform in the constrained space (x), although not uniform in the unconstrained space (w). I don't know what to do from here, you can concentrate the distribution of w with some prior to get more efficient sampling, but then the distribution of x would not be uniform among positive solutions to Ax = b. Maybe someone else has an idea.

Ben

parts:
As I noted in my longer write up, the positive solutions to Ax = b with dim(x) = N, dim(b) = M are given by the intersection of M simplices,
which (I believe, but don’t quote me) will be a (N - M) dimensional simplex.   You should be able to prove this using the pseudo-inverse
construction from Wikipedia that Ben quoted (immediately the solution lies on the intersection of M hyperplanes, you just have to show
that the intersection is nonzero and when it is nonzero the constrains imply that the intersection is a simplex).

The hard part here is not sampling from the solution space but defining the solution space.  Sampling once it has been defined is the
easy part here.

Thanks for your reply, Mr. Betancourt!

Yes, MCMC is too big a tool if all I want is sampling from simplex, but I want to sample from the positive solutions of Ax=b. Could you provide some further guidance on "but could be worked out analytically" or other viable options?

Yuanchu

On Tuesday, July 29, 2014 4:45:08 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
I’m not sure I understand why Stan would be the right choice for this — in the case of a single
column-A matrix and positive x you can construct the simplex analytically and sample from
a Dirichlet over that simplex directly, using the usual normalized gamma variates (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution#Random_number_generation) or
(n - 1) draws from a Beta distribution (http://arxiv.org/abs/1010.3436).  MCMC shouldn’t
be necessary for this relatively simple problem.

In the case of multiple constraints you have to figure out the constrained space (the intersection
of multiple simplices) which Stan wouldn’t be able to do anyways, but could be worked out
analytically with enough effort.
